## Start with the chemical potential {#chemical-potential}

Follow the same reaction throughout the derivation.

$$\mathrm{A_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 2A(g)}$$

The chemical potential of each species depends on its activity.

$$\mu_i=\mu_i^\circ+RT\ln a_i$$

$\mu_i^\circ$ refers to the chosen standard state. The activity $a_i$ is dimensionless. For a gas, use $a_i=f_i/p^\circ$.

::: {.notes}
เริ่มที่ chemical potential ของสารแต่ละชนิด แยกส่วนมาตรฐานกับส่วนที่ขึ้นกับ activity ให้เห็นก่อน activity ของแก๊สใช้ fugacity หารด้วยความดันมาตรฐาน จึงไม่มีหน่วย
:::

## Combine the potentials along the reaction {#reaction-gibbs-energy}

At fixed temperature and pressure, a small forward reaction consumes one unit of A₂ and forms two units of A.

$$\mathrm dn_{\mathrm A}=2\,\mathrm d\xi,\qquad \mathrm dn_{\mathrm{A_2}}=-\mathrm d\xi$$

Substitute these amounts into $\mathrm dG=\sum_i\mu_i\,\mathrm dn_i$.

$$\mathrm dG=(2\mu_{\mathrm A}-\mu_{\mathrm{A_2}})\,\mathrm d\xi$$

The reaction Gibbs energy is the slope along the reaction extent $\xi$.

$$\Delta_rG=\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial\xi}\right)_{T,P}=2\mu_{\mathrm A}-\mu_{\mathrm{A_2}}$$

::: {.notes}
เลขสองและเครื่องหมายลบมาจากสมการปฏิกิริยา อธิบายว่า delta-r-G เป็นความชันของ G ต่อความก้าวหน้าปฏิกิริยา ณ องค์ประกอบขณะนั้น
:::

## The activity ratio is Q {#reaction-quotient}

Insert $\mu_i=\mu_i^\circ+RT\ln a_i$ into the reaction Gibbs energy.

$$\Delta_rG=(2\mu_{\mathrm A}^\circ-\mu_{\mathrm{A_2}}^\circ)+RT(2\ln a_{\mathrm A}-\ln a_{\mathrm{A_2}})$$

Define $\Delta_rG^\circ=2\mu_{\mathrm A}^\circ-\mu_{\mathrm{A_2}}^\circ$ and combine the logarithms.

$$\Delta_rG=\Delta_rG^\circ+RT\ln\left(\frac{a_{\mathrm A}^2}{a_{\mathrm{A_2}}}\right)$$

The ratio calculated from the mixture's **current activities** is the reaction quotient.

$$Q=\frac{a_{\mathrm A}^2}{a_{\mathrm{A_2}}},\qquad \Delta_rG=\Delta_rG^\circ+RT\ln Q$$

::: {.notes}
ชี้การรวม logarithm ให้เห็นว่า activity ของผลิตภัณฑ์อยู่ข้างบน ของสารตั้งต้นอยู่ข้างล่าง และยกกำลังตามสัมประสิทธิ์ Q ใช้สภาวะขณะนี้ จะอยู่ที่สมดุลหรือยังดำเนินปฏิกิริยาก็ได้
:::

## At equilibrium, Q equals K {#equilibrium-constant}

At reaction equilibrium, $\Delta_rG=0$. Call the equilibrium value of the activity ratio $K$.

$$0=\Delta_rG^\circ+RT\ln K,\qquad K=\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta_rG^\circ}{RT}\right)$$

For the written reaction and chosen standard states, the temperature determines $K$. Combine this relation with the expression for the current mixture.

$$\boxed{\Delta_rG=RT\ln\left(\frac{Q}{K}\right)}$$

Compare $Q$ with $K$ to predict the reaction direction. Which sign does $\Delta_rG$ have when $Q<K$?

::: {.notes}
ตอนนี้จึงใช้เงื่อนไขสมดุล delta-r-G เท่ากับศูนย์ เรียกค่าอัตราส่วนที่สมดุลว่า K จากนั้นแทนกลับเพื่อได้ RT ln Q/K ให้นิสิตบอกว่า Q น้อยกว่า K ทำให้ logarithm ติดลบ จึงเดินหน้า
:::

## Q and K for the same reaction {#q-and-k}

For $\mathrm{A_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 2A(g)}$, use the dimensionless activity ratio $a_{\mathrm A}^2/a_{\mathrm{A_2}}$.

**Reaction quotient, $Q$.** Calculate the ratio using the activities in the mixture *now*.

**Equilibrium constant, $K$.** At equilibrium the ratio equals $K$. Its value is fixed at a given temperature for the written reaction and chosen standard states.

| If $Q<K$ | If $Q=K$ | If $Q>K$ |
|---|---|---|
| The forward reaction forms A. | The reaction is at equilibrium. | The reverse reaction forms A₂. |

::: {.notes}
ชี้ที่อัตราส่วนเดียวกัน ถ้าใส่ activity ตอนนี้จะได้ Q ถ้าใส่ค่าที่สมดุลจะได้ K จากนั้นให้ลองบอกทิศปฏิกิริยาเมื่อ Q ต่ำกว่า K ก่อนเริ่มโจทย์อัดแก๊ส
:::

## Does doubling the pressure always double Q? {#week5-questions}

**A question from Week 5.** How does the pressure argument change for a real gas?

Start with the ideal-gas reaction $\mathrm{A_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 2A(g)}$. At 350 K, $K=3.953$ for $p^\circ=100$ kPa. Compress the mixture from 100 to 200 kPa at fixed temperature. Consider the instant before the composition responds.

| Starting value | Predict $Q$ immediately after compression | Which way will the reaction move? |
|---|---|---|
| $Q=K=3.953$ | Calculate on paper | Toward A or A₂? |
| $Q=1.000$ | Calculate on paper | Toward A or A₂? |

Take one minute. Compare your two answers with a neighbor.

## Compare the new quotient with K {#pressure-check}

At fixed mole fractions, the ideal-gas quotient for this reaction is proportional to pressure.

$$Q=\frac{y_{\mathrm A}^2}{y_{\mathrm{A_2}}}\frac{P}{p^\circ}$$

| Before compression | Immediately after | Response at 350 K |
|---|---|---|
| $Q=3.953$ | $Q=7.906>K$ | More A₂ forms. |
| $Q=1.000$ | $Q=2.000<K$ | More A forms. |

As the reaction proceeds, the mole fractions change. At the new equilibrium, $Q=K=3.953$ in both cases.

::: {.notes}
Thai spoken recap: ความดันเพิ่มทำให้ Q ของปฏิกิริยานี้เพิ่มทันทีเมื่อองค์ประกอบยังคงเดิม ทิศทางขึ้นกับว่า Q ใหม่สูงหรือต่ำกว่า K.
:::

## A real gas uses fugacity in each activity {#real-gas}

At a specified $T,P,\mathbf y$, a mixture equation of state gives each component's fugacity coefficient $\phi_i$. With an ideal-gas standard state,

$$a_i=\frac{f_i}{p^\circ}=\frac{\phi_i y_iP}{p^\circ},\qquad Q=\frac{a_{\mathrm A}^2}{a_{\mathrm{A_2}}}.$$

For this dissociation, the multiplier on the ideal-gas estimate is $\phi_{\mathrm A}^2/\phi_{\mathrm{A_2}}$. The coefficients can change during compression and as the reaction proceeds. The same $T$, written reaction and standard states give the same $K$.

**Try it.** At 350 K and 200 kPa, use $y_{\mathrm A}=0.80$, $y_{\mathrm{A_2}}=0.20$. For this illustrative state take $\phi_{\mathrm A}=0.90$ and $\phi_{\mathrm{A_2}}=0.95$. Calculate both activities and predict the direction.

## Work the real-gas example on paper {#real-gas-check}

The pressure ratio is $200/100=2$. At the specified composition,

| Quantity | Calculation | Value |
|---|---|---:|
| $a_{\mathrm A}$ | $0.90(0.80)(2)$ | 1.44 |
| $a_{\mathrm{A_2}}$ | $0.95(0.20)(2)$ | 0.38 |
| $Q$ | $1.44^2/0.38$ | 5.46 |

The ideal-gas estimate at this same state is $6.40$. Both exceed $K=3.953$, so A₂ forms. To find the final extent for the real gas, update the composition and both fugacity coefficients until $Q=K$. Lab 12 solves the ideal-gas case.

::: {.notes}
Thai spoken recap: ใช้ fugacity แทนความดันย่อยในการหาค่า activity ของแก๊สจริง เมื่อคำนวณ Q แล้วให้เปรียบเทียบกับ K ที่อุณหภูมิเดียวกัน ตัวอย่างนี้ให้ Q เท่ากับ 5.46 จึงเกิด A₂ เพิ่มขึ้น.
:::

## Week 2 · What did the VLE measurement tell us? {#review-week-2}

A VLE measurement gives $P=100$ kPa, $x_1=0.40$, $y_1=0.60$. Assume an ideal vapor, negligible Poynting correction and a pure-liquid reference state.

$$y_1P=x_1\gamma_1 P_1^{\rm sat},\qquad a_1=x_1\gamma_1.$$

1. Use $P_1^{\rm sat}=120$ kPa. Find $\gamma_1$ and $a_1$.
2. A second source gives 150 kPa at the same temperature. Predict which way your inferred $\gamma_1$ moves.
3. Before fitting the data, which Antoine conventions would you check?

::: {.notes}
Allow three minutes for pairs. Check 1.25 and 0.50, then 1.00 and 0.40. Ask about the log base, temperature unit, pressure unit and correlation range. Thai spoken recap: ข้อมูลทดลองชุดเดิมให้ค่า activity coefficient ต่างกันได้ ถ้าใช้ความดันไออิ่มตัวต่างกัน ต้องตรวจหน่วยและช่วงอุณหภูมิของสมการ Antoine.
:::

## Week 3 · Would this feed split into two liquids? {#review-week-3}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="53%"}
![Mixing Gibbs energy and the supporting common tangent for the Week 3 Margules liquid at A=3.](figures/gibbs-review-curve.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="At feed z=0.12 the supporting common tangent lies below the homogeneous liquid Gibbs curve."}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
At $z_1=0.12$, compare the curve and the supporting line at the **same overall composition**. Which state has lower Gibbs energy?

The homogeneous curve has positive local curvature here. What does the tangent tell you that curvature alone cannot?

A Gibbs–Duhem area test examines the VLE data. How could errors of opposite sign affect its signed integral?
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The split lies below the homogeneous point, despite the positive local curvature. At the same T and P the split meets the same material balance. Local residuals of opposite sign can cancel in an area integral. Thai spoken recap: การตรวจความสอดคล้องของข้อมูลกับการตรวจว่าเฟสเสถียรตอบคนละคำถาม ที่องค์ประกอบรวมเดียวกันให้เลือกสถานะที่พลังงานกิบส์ต่ำกว่า.
:::

## Week 4 · Can the vessel supply that much gas? {#review-week-4}

At 300 K, a 1.00 L vessel contains 0.00200 mol of volatile A. Its equilibrium sublimation pressure is 10.0 kPa. Use $R=8.314$ kPa L mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ and assume an ideal gas.

1. Calculate the gas inventory required for $P_A=10.0$ kPa. Will any bulk solid remain?
2. Calculate the actual $P_A$. What happens to $P_A$ if you add an inert gas at fixed $T,V$?
3. In a separate adsorption vessel, an adsorbent of mass $m_s$ holds $q(P_A,T)$ mol per kg. Which term must you add to the gas inventory to close the balance?

::: {.notes}
Hold the free gas volume fixed and assume the inert does not adsorb. Thai spoken recap: ต้องมีสารมากพอจึงจะเหลือของแข็งและได้ความดันระเหิด ถ้ามีตัวดูดซับให้รวมจำนวนโมลบนผิวในสมดุลมวลด้วย.
:::

## Week 5 · Change pressure, then change temperature {#review-week-5}

Lab 12 used 1 mol of A₂ initially, zero A, no inert, and $p^\circ=100$ kPa. Use the same ideal-gas reaction in all three cases.

| Case | $T$ (K) | $P$ (kPa) | $K$ | Equilibrium extent (mol) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 12A | 350 | 100 | 3.953 | 0.7050 |
| 12B | 350 | 400 | 3.953 | 0.4451 |
| 12C | 400 | 100 | 33.861 | 0.9457 |

Which pair isolates pressure? Which isolates temperature? For 12C assume a constant positive reaction enthalpy of 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Explain the change in $K$.

With a partner, use the extent in 12B to check $2n_{\mathrm{A_2}}+n_{\mathrm A}$ against the feed.

| 2 · VLE | With $P_1^{\rm sat}=120$ kPa, $\gamma_1=1.25$ and $a_1=0.50$. With $P_1^{\rm sat}=150$ kPa they become 1.00 and 0.40. Check Antoine units, log base and temperature range. |

Ask one pair per row and collect one remaining question before moving on. Thai spoken recap: ในทุกกรณี เริ่มจากกำหนดสถานะอ้างอิงและเงื่อนไขที่ตรึงไว้ แล้วตรวจสมการสมดุลควบคู่กับสมดุลมวล.

## The question for today {#the-question-for-today}

What determines the sign of a concentration-cell potential?

Week 5 gave us $\Delta_rG=RT\ln(Q/K)$. A reversible cell turns that reaction driving force into a potential difference, $E=-\Delta_rG/(nF)$.

**Predict on paper.** For the reaction as written, what sign should $E$ have when $Q<K$? What voltage would you measure at complete cell equilibrium, $Q=K$?

[Pre-class reading and preparation questions](files/preclass-week-06.pdf)

## Two reduction half-reactions

Enter both half-reactions as reductions. Reverse the left reaction and add the right after matching electron counts.

$$E_{cell}^\circ=E_{right}^\circ-E_{left}^\circ$$

Both potentials need the same reference electrode and temperature. Multiplying a half-reaction does not multiply its potential.

## Nernst equation from reaction thermodynamics

Combine ΔrG=ΔrG°+RTlnQ with ΔrG=−nFE:
$$E=E^\circ-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$$

At 298.15 K,
$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.05915935\ \mathrm V}{n}\log_{10}Q$$

Changing T requires valid E° data at the new T.

## A concentration-cell calculation

Use the same $\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}$ couple on both sides at 298.15 K. For oxidation on the left and reduction on the right, $Q=a_{\mathrm L}/a_{\mathrm R}$. Take $a_{\mathrm L}=0.01$, $a_{\mathrm R}=1$, $n=2$, and neglect the junction potential.
$$Q=0.01,\qquad E=+0.05915935\ \mathrm V$$

E°=0, K=1, but E is nonzero. Reversing the concentrations changes the sign of E. Equal activities give E=0.

ΔrG≈−11.416 kJ per mol of the written reaction.

## An independent check

Use dimensionless activities. Concentration is an approximation with a stated standard concentration and activity coefficient.

Use Eright−Eleft and deltaG=−nFE with the balanced electron count. Equal activities must give zero potential for the same reduction couple.
